description.narrative: Peru propose to carry out 4 key strategies by 2024: 1) strengthening the technical capacities and soft skills of rural and agrarianwomen and their communities in order to contribute to improving their resilience and capacity to face the structural problems that affect them as part of the agrarian sector, 2) strategic communication to raise awareness in digital spaces of narratives in favor of agroecological practices of family and peasant agriculture, especially rural women (for example, through the platform Actúa.pe platform), and the generation and dissemination of evidence from a journalistic approach that can account for the barriers faced by family and peasant agriculture. This first year is also expected to generate evidence and dialogues prior toCOP30 that will consolidateproactive messages, seeking to show that for systemic change it is essential to consolidate an agroecological production model and position the voices and knowledge of rural women. 3) enabling access to strategic spaces for multilevel social and political advocacy that seeks to influence agrarian and environmental policies, as well as access to national and international climate finance, 4) strengthening national-level articulation and political leadership of women, their communities and agrarian organizations to effectively address structural challenges from the local to the global level and promote a focus on territorial, social and environmental justice in the agrarian sector. With a 4-year horizon, our implementing partneris Fomento para la Vida (FOVIDA), a nationwide institution that works in rural areas, promoting agroecology and with it: the recovery and adoption of agroecological practices by small farmers, associativity, conservation of native seeds and conservationoffragile ecosystems. It also promotes political processes in theterritories, training and strengthening leadership skills in women, men and youth, seeking to develop models for adaptation to climate change in rural communities. In addition, a national coalition of farmers' organizations, led by SD=CS, will participate. Through this coalition, small farmers' issues and the need to recognize traditional seed systems and farmers' rights have been placed on the public agenda. For this reason, national agrarian organizations will be key allies for the intervention. The National Agrarian Confederation (CNA), the National Convention of Peruvian Agriculture (CONVEAGRO), the National Federation of Peasant, Artisan, Indigenous, Native and Salaried Women of Peru (FENMUCARINAP), and other regional organizations have joined together in the Native Seed Promotion Group (Grupo Impulsor de Semillas Nativas), This is a platform from which they have advocated for the recognition of traditional seed systems and integratedother demands related to making visible and valuing the contribution of peasant women, demanding financing for measures to adapt to climate change and promoting a program for agroecological transition and organic agriculture.

participating-org.narrative:
Peru is a country in which poverty and, above all, inequality continue to be central problems, despite progress made in macroeconomic terms over the past two decades.
The economy has grown overall, mainly due to increasing exports of raw materials. This has put pressure on natural resources, violated the rights of poor populations in rural and urban areas, weakened democracy and overlooked structural problems that foster the exclusion of the majority of the population.
Of extreme concern is the existing gap in the levels of poverty between urban and rural areas. The poorest sectors continue to be concentrated in rural areas, principally in the southern highlands. The extreme poverty rate of populations with a primary language other than Spanish is three times greater than the national average and in the same rural areas extreme poverty is almost twice as high for those who do not speak Spanish as a first language.
Many business practices, above all in extractive industries, and disinterest on the part of the Peruvian State to adopt inclusive development practices contribute to socio-environmental and labor conflicts in the country and a marked discrimination towardsindigenous populations.
Movements against the status quo are emerging in the region, defending the rights of people to decide about their ways of life. Indigenous peoples and their organizations have built regional networks from where they construct proposals consolidated in the notion of “El buen vivir” (Living Well). These proposals pose an alternative indigenous worldview based on community life and the respect for nature, preserving life on the planet on the basis of recognition of their “cosmovision” and the respectfor cultural pluralism.
Oxfam in Peru Oxfam in Peru is contributing to this change by fostering these movements and promoting dialogue and action through the following thematic areas:
Economic justice: We aim to build the capacity of small farmers and indigenous populations of the Andes and Amazon to achieve sustainable livelihoods and help them attain recognition over land and natural resources through the adoption and implementation of favorable policies by the Peruvian State. We aim to secure the rights of communities affected by extractive industries bypromoting consultation processes, defense of territory, access to information, and participation in decision-making spaces. Citizenship, gender justice and interculturality: We support women, youth, and indigenous people to become active citizens and reverse gender discrimination and violence. Through their organizations, women work to build and position proposals that guarantee their participation in the formulation of public policies affecting access and control over their resources.In doing so, theyalso promote the importance of dialogue among different stakeholders and respect for the diversity of identities. Humanitarian response and disaster risk reduction: We work with poor and vulnerable communities - with a focus on women - so that they may better participate in advocacy processes that support their right to protection against disasters and their access to effective humanitarian assistance. The GROW campaign is very present in Peru, where multiple activities are being conducted related to foodjustice, which are approached from the perspective of the three themes mentioned.
